title: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (India)
specialty: Infectious Diseases / Occupational Health / Emergency Medicine

evidenceAudit.scope: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) after occupational (needlestick, splash) and non-occupational (sexual, including sexual assault) exposure in India: first aid, risk assessment, timing, the three-drug regimen, baseline and follow-up tests, hepatitis B and C, and transition to pre-exposure prophylaxis. The NACO National Guidelines for HIV Care and Treatment (2021) section 2.10 could not be opened, so WHO (2024), CDC (2025) and the WHO-prequalified TLD label are used.
findings: Start as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours; 28-day course; three drugs preferred (WHO 2024 summary).

Dolutegravir plus tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine as a preferred regimen; baseline HIV, hepatitis B, creatinine, ALT, AST and pregnancy tests; HIV testing at 4–6 and 12 weeks (CDC 2025, Appendix A).

TLD (dolutegravir/lamivudine/tenofovir DF 50/300/300 mg) one tablet daily for 28 days for PEP, 30 kg or more; not with creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min; dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily with rifampicin; separate from cations (WHO PQ label HA737).

Paediatric dolutegravir weight bands and PEP dosing checked against the WHO-prequalified dispersible label (HA793); lamivudine, tenofovir and zidovudine paediatric doses against NYSDOH Table A1 (December 2025); HBIG 0.06 mL/kg, vaccine 1 mL (0.5 mL under 19) at 0, 1, 6 months, and HCV RNA at 4–6 weeks against the Kasturba Hospital guideline.
unverifiedSections: NACO 2021 Tables 2.10.6–2.10.11 (exposure and source codes, regimens, follow-up) could not be read; NACO-specific regimens and codes are not shown.

Children under 30 kg: no single source opened gives a complete paediatric PEP regimen; the regimen here combines the WHO-prequalified dolutegravir dispersible label (PEP dosing) with NYSDOH paediatric doses of lamivudine, zidovudine and tenofovir.
Hepatitis B PEP (HBIG 0.06 mL/kg and vaccine schedule) and first aid are from the Kasturba Hospital, Manipal occupational PEP guideline, not the national NACO tables.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: PEP is a 28-day course of antiretroviral therapy (ART) started soon after a possible exposure to HIV to stop infection becoming established. Health workers in India are at risk from needlestick and sharps injuries, and PEP is also needed after sexual exposure and sexual assault. It works best within hours and is not started after 72 hours. Care includes immediate first aid, assessing the exposure and the source, baseline testing, a three-drug regimen (dolutegravir with tenofovir and lamivudine as a single TLD tablet in India), adherence support, follow-up HIV testing, and hepatitis B and C assessment. People with ongoing risk can move straight on to pre-exposure prophylaxis. The same visit also deals with hepatitis B, for which vaccination and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) are highly effective, and hepatitis C, for which there is no prophylaxis but early detection allows cure.
keyMechanisms: HIV first infects local cells and reaches lymph nodes over 24–72 hours.
Early ART can block viral replication before infection is established.
Integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir) block viral DNA integration; tenofovir and lamivudine block reverse transcriptase.
Risk depends on fluid, route, depth of injury and source viral load.

clinicalManagement.title: First aid
actions: Wash wound with soap and water; do not squeeze or scrub; flush splashes to eyes or mouth with water.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Type of exposure and fluid; source status if known.
Exposure within 72 hours and risk present: start PEP as early as possible; PEP works best when started early (WHO 2024).

clinicalManagement.title: Start PEP
actions: TLD one tablet daily for 28 days (label).
Sexual exposure: emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg) and STI treatment (see STI topics); tetanus cover for wounds after assault.

clinicalManagement.title: Hepatitis B and C
actions: Check worker's vaccination and anti-HBs; give HBIG 0.06 mL/kg and start vaccine if source HBsAg positive and worker non-immune (Kasturba guideline).
Hepatitis C source: no PEP; HCV RNA at 4–6 weeks and refer if positive (Kasturba guideline).

clinicalManagement.title: Follow-up
actions: Ongoing risk: move straight to pre-exposure prophylaxis (CDC 2025).

vignette.text: A 24-year-old staff nurse at a medical college hospital in Pune sustains a deep needlestick injury while recapping a hollow-bore needle after drawing blood from a patient on the medical ward. The patient's HIV status is unknown, and he was admitted with weight loss and oral candidiasis. The nurse completed two doses of hepatitis B vaccine as a student but never had her anti-HBs checked. She reports 40 minutes after the injury.

guidedApproach.title: Why timing decides everything
guidedApproach.prompt: Why must PEP start within hours rather than days?
guidedApproach.guidance: After a percutaneous or mucosal exposure, HIV first infects dendritic cells and T cells at the site, then reaches regional lymph nodes and the bloodstream over roughly 24–72 hours. Antiretroviral drugs can stop this local replication before the infection becomes established, but once the virus has disseminated and integrated into host DNA, a short course cannot clear it. This is why WHO advises starting ideally within 24 hours and never after 72 hours, and why the first dose should be given before source results are available. A three-drug regimen is preferred because it suppresses replication more completely, and dolutegravir is chosen as the third drug because it is potent, well tolerated and has a high barrier to resistance.

guidedApproach.title: Assessing the exposure and the source
guidedApproach.guidance: Risk depends on the fluid, the route and the source. Blood and visibly blood-stained fluids carry the highest risk; deep injuries with a hollow-bore needle that was in a vein or artery carry more risk than a solid suture needle. Exposure of intact skin needs no PEP. Mucosal splashes and non-intact skin need PEP if the source is HIV positive or unknown. For sexual exposure, including sexual assault, condomless receptive anal or vaginal sex carries the highest risk. The source should be tested with consent, but PEP is started at once and stopped only if the source is shown to be HIV negative without a recent risk. Every exposure is also a hepatitis B and hepatitis C exposure.

guidedApproach.title: The baseline and follow-up tests
guidedApproach.prompt: What do you test, and when?
guidedApproach.guidance: At the first visit, test the exposed person for HIV to make sure they were not already infected, because a reactive result changes management to HIV treatment. Check hepatitis B status (HBsAg and anti-HBs), hepatitis C antibody, creatinine and transaminases for drug safety, and a pregnancy test where relevant. Follow-up HIV testing is at 4–6 weeks and again at 12 weeks; hepatitis C RNA at 4–6 weeks is used when the source is hepatitis C positive, because there is no prophylaxis and early infection can be cured. Advise condoms until follow-up tests are negative.

guidedApproach.title: Choosing and completing the regimen
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you give PEP to adults and to children?
guidedApproach.guidance: For adults and adolescents of 30 kg or more, the single-tablet combination of dolutegravir, lamivudine and tenofovir (TLD) once daily for 28 days is simple and well tolerated; separate it from antacids, calcium and iron, and check that creatinine clearance is at least 50 mL/min. Children under 30 kg need weight-based dolutegravir dispersible tablets with lamivudine and a second nucleoside (tenofovir from 2 years and 10 kg, or zidovudine for younger or smaller children), ideally under ART-centre supervision. Address hepatitis B at the same visit: a non-immune person exposed to an HBsAg-positive source needs HBIG 0.06 mL/kg and the vaccine course. Adherence support, side-effect review and follow-up testing are what make PEP effective.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 24-year-old nurse has a deep needlestick from a hollow-bore needle used on a patient of unknown HIV status who has oral candidiasis and weight loss. She presents 40 minutes later. Her baseline HIV test is non-reactive and creatinine is normal.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate action now?

options.text: Wait for the source patient's HIV result before deciding
options.explanation: Delay reduces effectiveness: PEP works best when started as early as possible, ideally within 24 hours (WHO 2024).

options.text: Start TLD one tablet daily for 28 days
options.explanation: Correct. Deep percutaneous exposure to a possibly HIV-positive source within 72 hours needs three-drug PEP, ideally started within hours.
Three drugs are preferred over two (WHO 2024).

options.text: No PEP because the risk from a needlestick is low
options.explanation: Deep injury with a hollow-bore needle is a high-risk exposure.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Start three-drug PEP immediately after a significant exposure.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Start within hours, never after 72 hours; 28 days; do not wait for the source.

boardQuestions.vignette: The same nurse received only 2 of the 3 hepatitis B vaccine doses as a student and has never had her anti-HBs checked. The source patient's tests return HBsAg positive and HIV non-reactive. Her own anti-HBs result today is below 10 mIU/mL and her HBsAg is negative.
boardQuestions.question: What should be given for hepatitis B?

options.text: Nothing, because she is partly vaccinated
options.explanation: Anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL means she is not protected.
A non-immune person exposed to an HBsAg-positive source needs immunoglobulin as well as vaccine.

options.text: Tenofovir for 28 days as hepatitis B prophylaxis
options.explanation: Tenofovir in TLD is for HIV PEP; hepatitis B prophylaxis is HBIG plus vaccine.

options.text: HBIG 0.06 mL/kg IM plus completion of the vaccine course
options.explanation: Correct. Source HBsAg positive and anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL: HBIG and vaccination (Kasturba guideline).
Waiting leaves her unprotected during the period of risk.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Manage hepatitis B exposure according to source status and the person's immunity.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Non-immune + HBsAg-positive source: HBIG 0.06 mL/kg plus vaccine.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 9-year-old girl weighing 24 kg is brought by her mother 30 hours after a sexual assault by an unknown adult. Her baseline HIV test is non-reactive and creatinine is normal. She can swallow small tablets. Child-protection services and the police have been informed, and she has been examined by a gynaecologist.
boardQuestions.question: Which regimen is most appropriate?

options.explanation: TLD is only for people weighing 30 kg or more (label).

options.text: Dolutegravir 50 mg film-coated daily with lamivudine 75 mg morning and 150 mg evening and tenofovir 200 mg daily, for 28 days
options.explanation: Correct. From 20 kg the film-coated 50 mg tablet is preferred when the child can swallow tablets; lamivudine 75/150 mg at 20–<25 kg and tenofovir 200 mg at 22–<28 kg (label; NYSDOH Table A1).

options.text: No PEP because more than 24 hours have passed
options.explanation: PEP can be started up to 72 hours.
Single-drug PEP is inadequate; three drugs are preferred.
A single drug is not PEP; a full regimen is needed.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Choose a weight-appropriate three-drug PEP regimen for a child.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Children under 30 kg: dolutegravir by weight + lamivudine + a second nucleoside, for 28 days.

patientEducation: Take the tablet at the same time daily for 28 days.
Use condoms until follow-up tests are negative.
